content: Imhotep, whose name is sometimes spelled as Immutef, Im-hotep, or Ii-em-Hotep, translates to the one who comes in peace. He was an Egyptian polymath who served under Pharaoh Djoser of the Third Dynasty as the chancellor to the king and the high priest of the sun god Ra at Heliopolis. Imhotep is widely regarded as the first architect and physician in recorded history whose name is known. His full list of titles includes: Chancellor of the King of Lower Egypt, First after the King of Upper Egypt, Administrator of the Great Palace, Hereditary Nobleman, High Priest of Heliopolis, Builder, Chief Carpenter, Chief Sculptor, and Maker of Vases in Chief. Imhotep was one of the very few mortals to be depicted as part of a pharaoh's statue and one of the rare commoners to be granted divine status after death. The center of his cult was located in Memphis. From the First Intermediate Period onward, he was also revered as a poet and philosopher. His sayings were famously referenced in ancient poems, such as: I have heard the words of Imhotep and Hordedef, with whose discourses men speak so much. The location of Imhotep's tomb has been lost to antiquity and remains unknown despite efforts to locate it. It is generally believed to be at Saqqara. Attribution of Achievements and Inventions Much of what is known about Imhotep is based on hearsay and conjecture. The ancient Egyptians credited him with numerous inventions, including the creation of the papyrus scroll, as he is considered its earliest known user. Architecture As an official under Pharaoh Djoser, Imhotep is believed to have designed the Pyramid of Djoser, also known as the Step Pyramid, at Saqqara around 2630–2611 BCE. He is also credited with the first known use of columns in architecture. Imhotep's contributions to Egyptian culture were so significant that his idealized image persisted well into the Ptolemaic period. The Egyptian historian Manetho attributed to him the invention of stone-dressed building methods during Djoser’s reign. However, while he was not the first to use stone in construction, he was the first to design a structure of the Step Pyramid's size entirely out of stone. Earlier examples of stone walling, flooring, lintels, and jambs existed sporadically during the Archaic Period, but the scale and ambition of the Step Pyramid were unprecedented. Medicine Imhotep is credited as the founder of Egyptian medicine and is believed to have authored a medical treatise that was remarkable for its lack of magical thinking. This text, known as the Edwin Smith Papyrus, contains anatomical observations, descriptions of ailments, and their treatments. The surviving papyrus is thought to have been written around 1700 BCE but may be a copy of texts that are a thousand years older. Birth Myths According to myth, Imhotep's mother was a mortal woman named Kheredu-ankh, who was later elevated to semi-divine status by claims that she was the daughter of the god Banebdjedet. Conversely, as the Son of Ptah, Imhotep was also mythologically linked to divine origins. Deification Imhotep was considered the inventor of healing and was sometimes said to have held up the goddess Nut, the personification of the sky, separating her from Geb, the personification of the earth, to prevent chaos. This act placed him in a divine role, and he was sometimes referred to as Nut's son. In artwork, he was also associated with the great goddess Hathor, who was later identified as the wife of Ra. Additionally, he was linked to Maat, the goddess embodying truth, cosmic order, and justice, as he was credited with creating and maintaining order out of chaos. Two thousand years after his death, Imhotep's status was elevated to that of a deity. He became the god of medicine and healing and was later associated with the Greek god Asclepius. In the region of Thebes, he was worshipped alongside Amenhotep, son of Hapu, another deified architect, as brothers. Over time, his prestige grew, and his temples during the Greek period became centers of medical teachings. Sir William Osler, a prominent figure in modern medicine, referred to Imhotep as the real Father of Medicine and the first physician to stand out clearly from the mists of antiquity. Famine Myth An inscription from Upper Egypt, dating to the Ptolemaic period, mentions a seven-year famine during Imhotep's time. According to the inscription, Pharaoh Djoser had a dream in which the Nile god spoke to him, and Imhotep is credited with preventing the famine. The parallels between this story and the biblical account of Joseph have long been noted. More recently, some alternative historians have suggested that Imhotep and Joseph may be the same individual, arguing that the supposed thousand-year gap between them reflects a flawed chronology.
